# Objects {#sec-engine-objects}

This chapter describes how the engine implements objects, the values of attributes whose type is an array type or
an object type. The chapters on the data model and the extensions define what such attributes mean; this chapter
assumes them.

The implementation separates two things. A *schema* states the value type of each value and the size of each fixed
array. An *object* holds the values themselves together with its geometry, that is, the size of each array and the
position of each value, and refers to the schema it belongs to. Schemas and geometries are trees of the same
recursive structure, and every algorithm in this chapter is a recursion over it.

The model library implements schemas, of class `BPMNOS::Schema`, in `model/utility/src/Schema.h`, objects in
`model/utility/src/Object.h`, and constants in `model/utility/src/ObjectRegistry.h` and
`model/utility/src/InputEncoder.h`. It declares the interface through which the execution library supplies schemas
in `model/bpmnos/src/SchemaProvider.h`.

## Schemas {#sec-engine-objects-schemas}

### Definition {#sec-engine-objects-types}

A *value type* is one of `boolean`, `integer`, `decimal` and `string`.

A *schema* is a value type, an array type or an object type. An *array type* consists of a schema, its *element
type*, and a *size*, which is either a number $n \geq 1$, in which case the array is *fixed*, or *open*. An *object
type* consists of one or more *fields*. A field consists of a name and a schema, its *type*.

Every attribute has a schema, its *attribute type*. An attribute whose type is an array type or an object type is
an *object attribute*, and its values are *objects*. Any other attribute holds a single value.

A fixed array of size $n$ has $n$ elements; the value of an open array determines its size. All elements of an
array have the same sizes. For example, in a value of `boolean[][]` all inner arrays have the same size.

### Representation {#sec-engine-objects-schema-members}

```cpp
enum ValueType { BOOLEAN, INTEGER, DECIMAL, STRING };
struct Schema;
struct ArrayType  { std::shared_ptr<const Schema> type; std::optional<size_t> size; };
struct Field      { std::string name; std::shared_ptr<const Schema> type; };
struct ObjectType { std::vector<Field> fields; };
struct Schema : std::variant<ValueType, ArrayType, ObjectType> { using variant::variant; };
```

A `Schema` is a `std::variant` of a `ValueType`, an `ArrayType` and an `ObjectType`, so that it is one of the
three, as the definition states; `std::holds_alternative` tells which, and `std::get` gives access to it. An
`ArrayType` holds its element type and its size, which is `std::nullopt` if the array is open. An `ObjectType`
holds its fields, and a `Field` holds its name and its type. An attribute holds its type as the member `Schema
type`.

A schema refers to the schemas it contains, the element type of an array and the types of the fields of an object,
through `std::shared_ptr<const Schema>`. A schema never changes once built, so a schema derived from another shares
every part it does not change.

Two schemas are equal, by `operator==`, if they describe the same type: the same value types, the same arrays with
the same sizes, and the same fields, in the same order and with equal types. The order of fields belongs to the
type, because it determines where each field is stored in an object. When the model is loaded, equality checks that
the sender and the recipient of a message state the same type, and that all definitions of an error, escalation or
signal of the same name do; their fields must therefore be declared in the same order.

### Notation {#sec-engine-objects-notation}

In the model, a schema is defined by a text in the notation

```
schema    := ( valuetype | object ) dimension*
object    := "{" field ( "," field )* "}"
field     := name ":" schema
dimension := "[" n "]" | "[]"
```

which is the text of the `type` field of an attribute. `Schema::parse` reads the text and creates the `Schema` it
defines. A value type or an object without dimensions defines that value type or object type. Each dimension adds
an array: `[n]` a fixed array of size $n$, `[]` an open array. The dimensions are written outermost first, so that
the text before them is the type of the innermost elements: `boolean[3][4]` is the array type of size 3 whose
element type is the array type of size 4 whose element type is `boolean`, and `grid[i][j]` has $i \leq 3$ and $j
\leq 4$. The schema `{ cost: decimal, flags: boolean[] }[]` is an open array whose element type is an object type
with the fields `cost`, of type `decimal`, and `flags`, an open array of `boolean`.

### Size declarations {#sec-engine-objects-size-declarations}

A *size declaration* states sizes for arrays in the type of an object attribute, for every instance of a scenario.
Applying it yields a new schema, a copy of the type in which these arrays are fixed at the stated sizes. A size
declaration is a row of the instance data whose initialisation contains no `:=`, which names no instance and has no
value in any other column. Its text is the name of the attribute followed by a path of steps. A step `[n]` states
the size $n$ for the next array, a step `[]` states no size for it, and a step `.name` descends into the field
`name`. For example, `facilities[6]` states the size 6 for the outer array of `facilities`, and
`facilities[].flags[3]` states the size 3 for the array `flags` in every element. Declarations for the same
attribute accumulate, so that these two together have the effect of `facilities[6].flags[3]`.

The node of a declaration determines the attribute it names. A declaration without a node names a global object
attribute or, if there is none of that name, the content of the signal of that name. A declaration with a node
names an object attribute the node declares or, if there is none of that name, the content of the message, error or
escalation the node throws. The content of a signal is declared only by the name of the signal, because a signal is
the same wherever it is thrown or raised; a declaration at a signal event is rejected, and so is a declaration of
content at a node that does not throw it.

`Schema::declareSizes` takes a schema and a declaration and returns a new schema. Along the path of the
declaration, the new schema has new parts, in which every array a step `[n]` names has the size $n$; every other
part it shares with the given schema. The function rejects a size of 0, a size contradicting one that the type or
an earlier declaration has fixed, an index step where the schema has no array, and an unknown field.

The instance data reader keeps, for every attribute a declaration names, the schema obtained so far, which is
initially its attribute type. Each declaration for the attribute replaces it by the schema `Schema::declareSizes`
returns for it. After the last declaration, this schema is the *effective schema* of the attribute. For a signal,
there is one such schema per signal name, which is the effective schema of the content at every node of the signal.
Without size declarations, the effective schema of an attribute is its attribute type.

`StaticDataProvider`, the base class of the other data providers, reads the instance data in two passes: the first
reads the size declarations, the second the values. Every effective schema is therefore complete before any value
is read.

The data provider holds the effective schemas for as long as it exists, and makes them available through the
interface `Model::SchemaProvider`. Its one function, `getSchema`, takes an object attribute and returns its
effective schema. The interface is declared in the model library, because the functions writing objects belong to
that library, which does not know the data provider; `Execution::DataProvider` implements it.

### Declared and effective schemas {#sec-engine-objects-schema-roles}

An object attribute has two schemas, which differ only in which arrays are fixed.

The *declared schema* is the attribute type stated in the model. The attribute holds it as `Attribute::type`, and
it is the same in every scenario.

The *effective schema* results from the declared schema by the size declarations of the instance data
(@sec-engine-objects-size-declarations). It may therefore differ between scenarios, and the data provider holds it.

The effective schema matters wherever it matters which arrays are fixed, that is, wherever an object of the
attribute is built or assigned. Wherever only value types and structure matter, the declared schema suffices, since
there it agrees with the effective schema.

## Values and objects {#sec-engine-objects-layout}

### Values {#sec-engine-objects-single-values}

A single value is represented by `Value`, that is `std::optional<number>`; `std::nullopt` is an undefined value. A
boolean is stored as 0 or 1, a string as its index in the string registry. Hence every value is a number, and a
`Value` does not know its value type. An attribute of a value type holds one `Value`.

A single value given to an attribute or to an element of an object whose value type differs is cast as in C++: to
`integer` by truncation towards zero, to `boolean` as 1 if the number is not 0 and as 0 otherwise, and to `decimal`
unchanged. A `string` is never cast, and nothing is cast to `string`. Arrays and objects are never cast.

### Objects {#sec-engine-objects-values}

The value of an object attribute is an *object*, of class `BPMNOS::Object`:

```cpp
struct Object {
  std::shared_ptr<const Layout> layout;
  std::vector<Value> values;
};
```

An object consists of a layout, which states its geometry and its schema, and the vector `values`, which holds
every value of the object, however deeply nested in arrays and fields, as a `Value`.

#### Layouts {#sec-engine-objects-layouts}

A *layout* represents the geometry of an object. It has the structure of a schema, with the actual size of every
array, and refers to the schema it lays out:

```cpp
struct Layout;
struct ArrayLayout  { std::shared_ptr<const Layout> layout; size_t size; };
struct FieldLayout  { size_t offset; std::shared_ptr<const Layout> layout; };
struct ObjectLayout { std::vector<FieldLayout> fields; };
struct Layout : std::variant<std::monostate, ArrayLayout, ObjectLayout> {
  std::shared_ptr<const Schema> schema;
  size_t size;
};
```

A `Layout` is a `std::variant` of a single value, `std::monostate`, an `ArrayLayout` and an `ObjectLayout`, and
adds the members `schema` and `size`. `Layout::size` is the number of positions a layout occupies in `values`, and
is not to be confused with `ArrayLayout::size`, the number of elements of an array. A single value, the alternative
`std::monostate`, has size 1. An array has `size` elements, all with the element layout `layout`, so its layout has
size $\mathit{size} \cdot \mathit{layout.size}$. An object has its fields in the order of the fields of its schema;
the `offset` of a field is the position of its first value relative to the first value of the object, that is, the
sum of the sizes of the layouts of the fields before it, and the size of the object's layout is the sum of the
sizes of the layouts of its fields.

`Layout::schema` is the *schema of the object*. A layout and its schema agree: the layout has the structure of the
schema, the schema states the value type of every single value and the name of every field, and every array that
the schema fixes has the size the schema states. The layout of an element or field refers to the corresponding part
of the schema, the element type or the type of the field. Hence the layout of any part of an object, together with
the values it covers, is itself an object of the corresponding part of the schema. An object knows its value types
through its schema, and no function that reads, renders or converts an object needs to be given the schema of the
object. Two layouts are equal if they have the same structure, sizes and offsets and their schemas are equal.

The values of an object are stored depth first: the elements of an array one after the other, and within an element
its fields in the order of the schema. The position of a value is therefore the sum of the displacements along the
path to it. An index $i$, counted from 1 as in expressions, displaces by $(i - 1) \cdot \mathit{layout.size}$,
where `layout` is the element layout of the array; a field name displaces by the offset of the field, which is
found at the position of the name among the fields of the schema.

For example, let `facilities` be of type `{ cost: decimal, flags: boolean[3] }[]`, in which `flags` is fixed at
size 3, and be assigned the value

```
[ { cost := 10.0, flags := [ true, false ] },
  { cost := 20.0, flags := [ false, false ] },
  { cost := 30.0, flags := [ true, true ] } ]
```

which gives only two flags per element. The outer array is open and has the size 3 of the value. The array `flags`
is fixed at size 3 in every element, so its third flag is undefined. The layout of the object is

```
array of 3 elements, size 12, schema { cost: decimal, flags: boolean[3] }[]
  element: object, size 4, schema { cost: decimal, flags: boolean[3] }
    cost:  offset 0, single value, size 1, schema decimal
    flags: offset 1, array of 3 elements, size 3, schema boolean[3]
      element: single value, size 1, schema boolean
```

and its values are

| Position | Path | Value |
|:-:|:--|:-:|
| 0 | `facilities[1].cost` | 10.0 |
| 1 | `facilities[1].flags[1]` | 1 |
| 2 | `facilities[1].flags[2]` | 0 |
| 3 | `facilities[1].flags[3]` | undefined |
| 4 | `facilities[2].cost` | 20.0 |
| 5 | `facilities[2].flags[1]` | 0 |
| 6 | `facilities[2].flags[2]` | 0 |
| 7 | `facilities[2].flags[3]` | undefined |
| 8 | `facilities[3].cost` | 30.0 |
| 9 | `facilities[3].flags[1]` | 1 |
| 10 | `facilities[3].flags[2]` | 1 |
| 11 | `facilities[3].flags[3]` | undefined |

The undefined flags occupy positions like any other value, so each element occupies 4 positions rather than 3, and
every position after the first element shifts accordingly. The position of `facilities[2].flags[2]` is

$$
\underbrace{(2 - 1) \cdot 4}_{\texttt{facilities[2]}} + \underbrace{1}_{\texttt{.flags}} +
\underbrace{(2 - 1) \cdot 1}_{\texttt{[2]}} = 6 .
$$

Since an array has one element layout, a size within its elements is the same in all elements and can only change
in all elements at once.

Like a schema, a layout refers to the layouts it contains through `std::shared_ptr<const Layout>`. A layout never
changes once built, so changing a size builds a new layout, which shares every part it does not change.

## Creating and assigning objects {#sec-engine-objects-creating}

### Building {#sec-engine-objects-schema-building}

An object can be built from a schema once the size of every array is known. A fixed array has its size. An open
array needs a size from elsewhere, and the two constructors below differ in where they take it from. The object
built belongs to the given schema.

```cpp
explicit Object(const Schema& schema);
Object(const Schema& schema, const nlohmann::json& json);
```

The first constructor builds an object from a schema alone. It gives every open array the size 0 and leaves every
value undefined. The result is the value of an object attribute that nothing has initialised. For the schema
`boolean[3]` it is an array of three undefined values; for `{ cost: decimal, flags: boolean[] }[]` it is an empty
array. It is explicit, so that a schema never converts to an object implicitly.

The second constructor builds an object from a schema and a parsed JSON value. It takes the sizes of the open
arrays from the JSON value and fills the object with its values. The size of an open array is the number of
elements of the JSON array at its position. Since all elements of an array have the same sizes, all JSON arrays at
the same position must have the same number of elements. A JSON number, truth value or text is a single value of
the value type the schema states at its position, and a JSON `null` stands for an undefined value.

### Converting {#sec-engine-objects-schema-conform}

An object given to an attribute, such as a literal or the object of another attribute, need not have the sizes the
attribute requires. A third constructor converts it:

```cpp
Object(const Schema& schema, const Object& source);
```

It builds an object of the schema `schema`, the *target*, from the object `source`, the *source*, whose schema is
the schema of its layout. It determines the layout of the new object by recursion over the target and the layout of
the source, with one rule for each of the three cases of a schema.

At a value type, the source must hold a single value of the same value type. Arrays and objects are not cast: their
values keep their value types, and a source whose value types differ from the target's is rejected.

At an array type, the source must be an array. If the target array is fixed at size $n$, the new array has size
$n$: a source with fewer elements is padded with undefined elements, and a source with more elements is cut off if
every value beyond the $n$-th element is undefined, and rejected otherwise. If the target array is open, the new
array has the size of the source. The element layout of the new array is determined by the same recursion from the
target's element type and the source's element layout.

At an object type, the source must be an object, and every field of the source must be a field of the target. Each
field of the new object is determined by the recursion from the field's type and the field of the source. A field
the source lacks is determined from its type alone, and every open array in it has size 0.

The constructor then copies the values of the source into the new object and leaves every other position undefined.
If the source cannot be converted, the constructor throws. For example, converting the literal `[ { cost := 10.0,
flags := [ true ] } ]` to `{ cost: decimal, flags: boolean[3] }[6]` builds an object of 24 values, of which only
the first cost and the first flag are defined.

No conversion is needed if every object of the source schema is, unchanged, an object of the target schema.
`Schema::supports`, called on the target with the source schema, tells whether this is the case. It holds if the
two schemas have the same structure, the same value types and the same fields in the same order, and if at every
array the target array is open or both arrays are fixed at the same size. A schema supports another only if the two
differ at most in which arrays are fixed.

Wherever an object is given to an attribute, the source is therefore kept if the target supports its schema, and
converted otherwise:

```cpp
slot = target.supports(*source->layout->schema) ? source : std::make_shared<Object>(target, *source);
```

A kept object keeps its layout and with it its schema, which may fix arrays that the target leaves open. For
example, the literal `[ 1, 2, 3 ]`, whose numbers are integers and which fixes no size, has the schema `integer[]`.
The schemas `integer[]` and `integer[3]` support it, so the literal is kept. The schema `integer[4]` does not, so
the literal is converted and padded. The schema `decimal[]` does not support it either, and the literal is
rejected; it must be written `[ 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 ]`.

### Schemas for assignment {#sec-engine-objects-schema-assignment}

An assignment to an existing object, to the whole object or to one of its elements, must not change the size of a
fixed array, but may change the size of an open array. The object assigned is therefore kept or converted
(@sec-engine-objects-schema-conform) for a *target schema*, which a constructor of `Schema` builds:

```cpp
Schema(const Schema& effectiveSchema, const Layout& currentLayout);
```

It is given the effective schema of the target of the assignment and the layout of the object currently there. For
an assignment to the whole object, these are the effective schema of the attribute and the layout of its object.
For an assignment to an element, they are the effective schema of the element, found by descending along the target
path, where an index descends into the element type and a field name into the type of the field, and the layout of
the element. The constructor builds a schema of the same structure, in which every array that is fixed in the
effective schema is fixed at the size it has in the current layout, and every open array stays open. The current
size is kept rather than the size the effective schema states, because a fixed array may have been resized during
the run; the array then remains fixed at its new size. The effective schema is needed rather than the schema of the
current object, because the current object may have been kept from a source whose schema fixes arrays that are open
in the effective schema.

Hence a fixed array keeps its size: a shorter source is padded with undefined elements, and a longer source is cut
off if only undefined values are cut, and rejected otherwise. For an attribute of type `integer[3]`, the literal `[
1, 2 ]` is padded with one undefined value, and the literal `[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]` is rejected. An open array takes the
size of the source: for an attribute of type `integer[]`, both literals are taken as they are.

In an assignment to an element, an open array within the element takes the size of the source as well. Since all
elements of the enclosing array share one element layout (@sec-engine-objects-layouts), the new size applies to
every element: the other elements are padded with undefined values or lose their values beyond the new size. For
example, if `flags` is open and has size 3 in every element of `facilities`, the assignment `facilities[2] := {
cost := 5.0, flags := [ true, false ] }` gives `flags` the size 2 in every element.

## Constants {#sec-engine-objects-constants}

A *literal* is written `[ ... ]` or `{ name := ... }`. `InputEncoder` replaces every literal by a number before the
text is parsed. It scans the text of every expression, of every initial value, and of every cell of the instance
data and of the inputs, once and from left to right. A quoted string becomes its index in the string registry. A
bracket opens a literal, except after a name, `]` or `)`, where it indexes, and after a membership operator, where
it encloses a set that the expression parser reads itself. A brace opens a literal if a name followed by `:=` comes
next.

`InputEncoder` reads a literal into a syntax tree. Each member is a string, a boolean, a number or a literal, and
its value type is stated by how it is written: `true` and `false` are `boolean`, a quoted text is `string`, a
number written with a decimal point, such as `1.0` or `2.5`, is `decimal`, and any other number, such as `1`, is
`integer`. The elements of an array must agree in value types, fields and sizes, so that `[ 1, 2.5 ]` is rejected
and must be written `[ 1.0, 2.5 ]`. From the tree, `InputEncoder` builds an object whose schema, the *constant
schema*, states the value types of the literal and leaves every array open, since a literal states no sizes. It
registers the object in the object registry, and replaces the literal by its registry index.
`InputEncoder::getObjectIndices` returns these indices in the order of the literals, so that an expression can tell
a constant from a number. `InputEncoder::getObjectIndex` returns the index if the whole text is a single literal,
and `std::nullopt` otherwise, so that an initial value can be recognised as a literal.

`InputEncoder::getEncodedInput` returns the input with every literal replaced by its number, which is the text that
is parsed afterwards. `InputEncoder::getEncodedLiterals` returns an `EncodedLiteral` for every literal of the
input, in their order. It states where the replacement of the literal begins and ends in the encoded input, and
whether the literal is a string, an object, or an object initialiser of the instance data, which is copied
unchanged. `CSVReader` uses them to split a line of a CSV file into cells: a cell that an encoded literal covers
exactly states that literal, and a delimiter within an object initialiser does not end a cell.

The *object registry*, the global `objectRegistry`, holds every constant, and `objectRegistry[i]` returns it. Equal
constants are registered once. Two constants are equal if their layouts, schemas included, and their values are
equal. The schemas take part because a string and a number may be held as the same number: `[ "a" ]` and `[ 0 ]`
differ, even if the string `a` has index 0.

The registry finds a constant by a hash of its schema, layout and values, and compares in full on equal hashes. Its
entries are stored in blocks of 4096, each allocated once and never moved. An atomic counter, raised only after an
entry is written, publishes the entries. Reading therefore takes no lock, and a reference to a constant remains
valid while further constants are registered. Only registration takes the mutex, so that concurrent registrations
of the same constant obtain one index.

Constants also arise from two sources when the model is loaded. Every lookup input of a data store becomes a
`LookupTable`, which `AttributeRegistry::lookupTables` holds under its name. Since LIMEX evaluates to numbers, a
lookup whose result column, its last column, has an array or object type returns the registry index of the constant
in the matching cell; every such cell must have value types equal to those of the column. When an expression is
compiled, it reads the schema of the result column from the table, and admits a lookup returning an object only as
the entire right side of an assignment to an object attribute. A matrix or object input of a data store is read
into one constant, which its `Input` holds together with the schema of the input, and its name is recorded in
`AttributeRegistry::inputs`. A matrix is read row by row into an array of arrays, an object input by the
constructor `Object(const Schema&, const nlohmann::json&)`.

An *object initialiser* in the instance data is a literal with expression members. `InputEncoder` does not register
it, because its values are known only after its members are evaluated. `ObjectInitializer` keeps its syntax tree
and the positions of its expression members, and `ObjectInitializer::instantiate` builds the object from the values
of the members. The value of an expression member is a single value, cast to the value type that the schema of the
attribute states at the position of the member; the other members follow the rules of literals.

## Attributes and storage {#sec-engine-objects-storage}

How the model initialises an attribute is held by one member:

```cpp
std::variant<std::monostate, size_t, std::unique_ptr<const Expression>> initialization;
```

It is `std::monostate` if the model gives no initial value. It is the registry index of a literal if the model
initialises an object attribute with a literal; the literal is checked by converting it to the declared schema. It
is the compiled assignment in every other case, which includes every initial value of an attribute of a value type
and an object attribute initialised, for instance, by a lookup. The assignment names its target, so it is compiled
only after the attribute is registered; until then, the constructor of `Attribute` keeps its text in a local
variable. An attribute whose initialization is not `std::monostate` is assigned by the model, and the instance data
must not give it a value. The instance and the timestamp are not object attributes, and object attributes do not
contribute to the objective.

The attribute registry numbers object attributes separately from the other attributes. `AttributeRegistry::add`
appends an object status attribute to `statusObjects` and an object data attribute to `dataObjects`, and the index
of an object attribute is its position there. The index of any other attribute therefore does not depend on object
attributes. As for the other data attributes, the global object attributes come first, followed by those of each
scope after those of its enclosing scopes. `Attribute::declaration` counts all attributes together in the order of
their declaration.

`Status` and `Data` each hold the vector `attributes`, with the values of the other attributes, and the vector
`objects`, with a `std::shared_ptr<const Object>` for each object attribute. The data chain `SharedData` refers to
both vectors of the data of a scope and of its enclosing scopes, outermost first. The constructor of `Data` from a
data chain copies the pointers.

`AttributeRegistry::getObject` returns a reference to the `std::shared_ptr<const Object>` that holds the object of
an attribute in the status or the data. It has two overloads: given a const status and const data, it returns a
const reference, for reading; given a non-const status and data, it returns a non-const reference, through which
the pointer can be replaced. `AttributeRegistry::setObject` replaces the object as a whole. It receives the
assigned object and the schema provider (@sec-engine-objects-size-declarations). It obtains the effective schema of
the attribute from the schema provider, and keeps or converts the assigned object for the target schema the
constructor of `Schema` builds from the effective schema and the current layout
(@sec-engine-objects-schema-assignment).

## Initialisation and lifetime {#sec-engine-objects-initialisation}

The data provider computes a *default* for every object attribute once. If the model initialises the attribute with
a literal, the default is the literal, kept or converted for the effective schema; otherwise it is the object the
constructor `Object(const Schema&)` builds from the effective schema. The default content object of a node stating
a message, signal, error or escalation is an undefined object of the effective schema of its content; all nodes of
a signal share the same one.

The instance data give an object attribute a value in a row that states a literal or an object initialiser. A
literal stands as its registry index. An object initialiser is evaluated over the values that earlier rows have
given. In both cases the object is kept or converted for the effective schema. A global object attribute takes its
value from the instance data if they give one, and otherwise its default. The stochastic data provider records the
objects of each instance in its scenario, so that a fork keeps what the run has revealed.

`InstanceValues` builds the values of a scope instance when the instance comes into being. For every object status
attribute and every object data attribute the scope declares, it appends the object the instance data give, or
otherwise the default. It then initialises the other attributes. Finally, it evaluates the initial expressions of
the object attributes in the order of their declaration, with the data provider as schema provider. When the ready
event of a process instance is processed, the engine moves the objects into the slots of the state machine of the
instance that follow the global objects. It moves them element by element, so that the references held by data
chains remain valid.

An object status attribute exists while the token is inside the scope declaring it. When the token leaves the
scope, its status is truncated by the status attributes the scope declares, the object status attributes included.
A token arriving at a compensation activity is truncated in the same way to the status of the enclosing scopes.

## Sharing {#sec-engine-objects-sharing}

Objects are copied often. A token is copied at a diverging gateway. The evaluators of a controller copy the data of
a token for every candidate decision. A controller may copy the system state to look ahead, and a fork copies its
scenario. Moreover, a default is given to every instance of its scope, and an operator assigns its literal every
time it is applied. Copying the values on each of these occasions would take time proportional to the number of
values, although most copies are never written.

Objects are therefore shared until they are written. Every holder holds a `std::shared_ptr<const Object>`, and
copying a status or data copies these pointers. An object is modified only through `BPMNOS::modifiable`. If the
pointer in the slot has a use count other than 1, this function first replaces the object in the slot by a copy; it
then returns the object for modification. An object held by one slot is thus written in place, and an object held
by several slots is copied at its first write. A constant is always copied, since the registry holds it as well.

Every object that may be modified is created non-const, as the constructors of `Object` do, and is held only
through pointers to const. This makes the cast in `BPMNOS::modifiable` well defined. A write takes its slot from
the status or data chain of its own token, so an evaluation that writes into copied data never alters the live
state.

An object is kept wherever the target schema supports its schema (@sec-engine-objects-schema-conform), that is,
wherever the two schemas differ at most in which arrays are fixed. A literal, whose constant schema leaves every
array open, is thus kept by every attribute whose type has its value types and fields and whose arrays are open or
already have the sizes of the literal: the registry, the defaults derived from the literal, and every slot it is
assigned to then hold one and the same object. The object of an attribute is kept by every attribute whose type
supports its schema.

## Reading {#sec-engine-objects-reading}

An expression reads an object through a *path*, such as `facilities[i].cost`, `grid[i][j]`, or a name used as an
array. LIMEX parses a path into steps, each an index or a field name, and evaluates the indices. Resolving the path
is left to the caller, through the interface `LIMEX::Resolver`.

When an expression is compiled, `Expression::bindPaths` binds each path to the attribute or input it names and
checks it against the declared schema. An index must meet an array type and descends into its element type. A field
name must meet an object type and descends into the type of the field.

What a path must end at depends on how it is read. A path read as a value must end at a value type. A path read as
an array, that is, as the argument of an aggregator, on the right side of a membership operator, or in the binding
of an aggregation, must end at an array type whose element type is a value type. The argument of `size` may end at
any array type. A path inside an aggregation over an expression is marked to skip undefined values. Since strings
are held as indices, reading needs no value types at run time.

When an expression is evaluated, `Expression::execute` gathers the variables and the objects of the paths into
`thread_local` buffers, which every evaluation on the thread reuses, so that an evaluation does not allocate. A
`PathResolver` on the stack resolves each path with the function `locate`. It descends the layout along the path
and adds the displacement of each step: for an index $i$, counted from 1, $i - 1$ times the size of the element
layout; for a field name, the offset of the field. An index out of range or not integral is an error.

A path read as a value returns the value at the position reached. If that value or an index is undefined, the
expression is undefined; the resolver signals this by an exception local to `Expression.cpp`. A path marked to skip
undefined values returns NaN instead, which the aggregator ignores. A path read as an array returns a `LIMEX::View`
of the array. The values of the array are contiguous, since its elements are single values, and the view reads them
on demand without copying. For the argument of `size`, the view supplies only the size.

## Writing {#sec-engine-objects-writing}

Operators, initial expressions and ready expressions write objects through `Expression::writeToObject`, which
receives the status, the data and the schema provider. Writing an object does not change the objective.

When the expression is compiled, `Expression::analyseTarget` determines which of the four forms below the
assignment has. For a whole or element assignment, it also determines the source: a literal, an object attribute,
an input, a lookup returning an object, or a path to part of an object. Any other source is rejected. A compound
assignment such as `+=` is admitted only for a single value, and an object cannot be made undefined. Every source
is an object and carries its schema: a constant its constant schema, the object of an attribute or input the schema
of its layout, and the part of an object a path addresses the corresponding part of that schema.

A *resizing*, `resize(path) := n`, is rewritten into `path := n` before LIMEX parses it, and the path must end at
an array. `BPMNOS::resized` rebuilds the layout along the path with that array at size $n$. If the array is fixed
in the schema of the object, the rebuilt layout refers to a schema in which the array is fixed at size $n$, so that
layout and schema agree. If the array lies within the elements of an enclosing array, the element layout of the
enclosing array changes, so that the array changes in every element. The function `correspond` transfers the values
present in both layouts by recursion over both; dropped elements are lost and added elements are undefined. Whether
the array is fixed is stated by the effective schema, and resizing does not change it.

A *value assignment*, as in `facilities[i].cost := 5.0`, casts the evaluated value to the value type of the target
(@sec-engine-objects-single-values) and writes it into `modifiable(slot).values` at the position of the target
path. No size changes.

A *whole assignment*, as in `route := [ 1, 2, 3 ]`, is carried out by `AttributeRegistry::setObject`
(@sec-engine-objects-storage). If the target schema supports the schema of the source, the slot afterwards holds
the source itself. For a path source, a resolver records the indices of the source path instead of resolving it,
and the part of the object the path addresses, whose values are contiguous, is taken with its layout.

An *element assignment*, as in `grid[i] := [ 1, 2, 3 ]`, keeps or converts the source for the target schema built
from the effective schema of the element and the layout of the element (@sec-engine-objects-schema-assignment). If
an open array within the element thereby changes its size, `BPMNOS::resized` rebuilds the element layout of the
enclosing array, so that the size applies to every element. The values are then copied into the slot at the
position of the element.

## Merging and data updates {#sec-engine-objects-merging}

Tokens merge at a converging gateway and at the completion of a multi-instance activity. `Token::mergeStatus` then
merges each object status attribute by `BPMNOS::merge`. If all tokens hold the same object, that object is kept.
Otherwise the result has the layout of the objects if they all have the same layout, and else a layout built by
recursion, in which every array has the largest size it has in any of the objects. The merged objects belong to the
same attribute and therefore have the same value types and fields; in the schema of a built layout, an array is
fixed only where all objects fix it at the same size. Each value is merged by the rule for status values: the first
defined value is kept, an undefined value is no conflict, and a value differing from the one kept makes the result
undefined for good.

A data update reports an object as a whole. When the model is loaded, `ExtensionElements::dataUpdate` records the
data attributes that the operators and choices of a node may modify, object attributes included. The `DataUpdate` a
token notifies names the attribute, not its elements, so that conditional events and the cached candidates of a
controller treat a change of any element as a change of the object.

## Layouts during a run {#sec-engine-objects-relayout}

During a run, a new layout is built only where an object needs one that no object involved has. This happens in
five cases. First, a resizing sets the size of an array explicitly (@sec-engine-objects-writing). Second, an
element assignment changes the size of an open array within the elements (@sec-engine-objects-writing). Third, a
whole assignment combines sizes of different origins: the open arrays take the sizes of the source, while the fixed
arrays keep the sizes of the current object (@sec-engine-objects-schema-assignment), so that the result may have
the sizes of neither. Fourth, a merge combines objects of different sizes, and the result has the largest size of
each array (@sec-engine-objects-merging). Fifth, an object converted to a schema other than its own refers to that
schema, even where the sizes stay as they are, as the literal `[ 1, 2, 3 ]` converted to `integer[3]` does. The
second, third and fourth case are implicit resizings.

In every other case an existing layout is used. When the source is kept, it keeps its layout. The converting
constructor shares every part of the layout of the source that it would build unchanged, and a resizing and a merge
share every part they do not change. When the result of a whole assignment has the layout of the current object, as
after padding fixed arrays, `AttributeRegistry::setObject` gives it the layout of the current object. The part of
an object that a path addresses is taken with its sub-layout, and a merge of objects of equal layouts keeps their
layout. Writing a single value or copying an object never changes a layout.

## Content {#sec-engine-objects-content}

The content of a message, signal, error or escalation is an object of the object type its definition states. A node
stating such a definition has a *content attribute*. It is an object status attribute named after the message or
signal, created by a dedicated constructor of `Attribute` and registered in
`ExtensionElements::augmentedAttributeRegistry`, a copy of the attribute registry of the node against which the
operators of the node are compiled. Since it is registered after all object status attributes of that registry, its
index is their number. No other expression sees it. Its effective schema results from the size declarations for the
content (@sec-engine-objects-size-declarations), and the schema provider returns it like that of any other object
attribute.

`ExtensionElements::applyOperators` receives the schema provider, which it passes to every operator, and the
content object through a pointer. It appends the content object to the objects of the status, applies the
operators, and moves the content object back. The operators of a throwing node start from the default content
object of the node and leave the content they write in `Token::content`, from which the message or signal takes it.
The operators of a catching node may only read the content; a model in which such an operator writes it is rejected
when it is loaded. `Message` and `Signal` hold their content as a `Content`, the name together with a pointer to
the object, so that the content is shared with the throwing token until it is written.

## Rendering {#sec-engine-objects-rendering}

Rendering needs the value types, which the schema of the object states. `BPMNOS::to_json` renders an object by
recursion over its layout: an array as a JSON array, an object type as a JSON object with its fields in the order
of the schema, a boolean as a truth value, an integer as a JSON integer, a decimal as a JSON floating-point number,
a string as text, and an undefined value as `null`. `BPMNOS::to_string` renders an object in the notation of
literals, for error messages, so that the text it returns is a literal of the schema of the object: a decimal is
written with a decimal point, as `1.0` rather than `1`, and an integer without one. A single value of type
`decimal` is likewise written with a decimal point wherever it is rendered.

`Token::jsonify` builds the entries of the log. It collects the attributes of the status, the data and the globals,
orders them by `Attribute::declaration`, and renders each of them. `Message` and `Signal` render their content
object.
